results.summary: This design attempts to render metaballs on a VGA display. It outputs RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Silicon tests show partial functionality: one ball moves as expected, but the other exhibits erratic behavior, and results vary across chips. The documentation is minimal and the design is described as rushed.

This project implements a simple alarm clock with configurable alarm hours and minutes. It uses internal counters for hours and minutes, and asserts an alarm output when the current time matches the alarm setting. The design was sponsored by MITRE and MIT/LL Beaverworks Summer Institute, and includes a testbench for simulation. It uses both dedicated and bidirectional pins to accommodate all inputs and outputs.

This design is a 4-bit ALU slice intended for use in minicomputer or microcomputer CPUs. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 3-bit function code, and produces a 4-bit result along with carry, equal, and zero flags. The design was tested using an Altera FPGA. It provides basic arithmetic and logic functions.

This project implements a Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) unit using a Dadda multiplier and a Kogge-Stone adder. It is designed for digital signal processing tasks such as filtering and convolution. The design includes pipeline registers and an accumulator, and is verified with a provided testbench. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may be a documentation error.

This analog design implements two ring oscillators, one targeting 600 MHz and the other 300 MHz, with enable inputs and analog outputs. Silicon tests show that the first oscillator works at around 500 MHz with reduced amplitude, while the second oscillator is broken due to a missing via. The documentation notes that only analog outputs are connected, not digital ones.

This design is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter (DAC) with a 3.3V output, capable of being driven externally or by an internal sine waveform generator. Silicon tests confirm a smooth sine wave output over the full 3.3V range, with a slight nonlinearity at the mid-code transition. It requires an external multimeter to measure the output voltage. The design uses level shifting drivers to achieve the 3.3V output.

This design debounces inputs from three rotary encoders and generates PWM signals to control RGB LED brightness. It is intended for use with external digital encoders connected to the first six inputs. The project is a demo for the Zero to ASIC course. Testing involves twisting the encoders and observing the LED brightness changes.

This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker connected to the bidirectional pins in a differential PWM configuration. It requires an external piezo speaker or the Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod. The design also copies the input pins to the output pins for testing purposes. It operates with a 100 kHz clock and is intended for audio output.

This project implements a generic synchronous FIFO buffer with a single clock domain. It buffers data from an 8-bit input to an 8-bit output, with write and read enable signals and full/empty flags. The design is intended as an experimental microtile container. Testing involves writing data until full and reading until empty.

This design implements a maze game where the player can walk around and see adjacent walls on a 7-segment display. It uses the first four inputs to move up, down, left, or right. No external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout PCB. The documentation is minimal and does not provide details on the maze layout or game mechanics.
